text: I told him that I had just read a novel called American Psycho and that it was such a shame that young Americans were serial murderers. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, obviously I said this in a fit of mild irritation. <break time="0.8s" /> It would never have occurred to me to think that just because I had read a novel in which a character was a serial killer that he was somehow representative of all Americans. <break time="0.8s" /> And now, this is not because I am a better person than that student, but, because of Americas cultural and economic power, I had many stories of America. <break time="0.8s" /> I had read Tyler and Updike and Steinbeck and Gaitskill. <break time="0.8s" /> I did not have a single story of America. <break time="0.8s" /> When I learned, some years ago, that writers were expected to have had really unhappy childhoods to be successful, I began to think about how I could invent horrible things my parents had done to me. <break time="0.8s" /> But the truth is that I had a very happy childhood, full of laughter and love, in a very close knit family. <break time="0.8s" /> But I also had grandfathers who died in refugee camps. <break time="0.8s" /> My cousin Polle died because he could not get adequate healthcare. <break time="0.8s" /> One of my closest friends, Okoloma, died in a plane crash because our firetrucks did not have water. <break time="0.8s" /> I grew up under repressive military governments that devalued education, so that sometimes my parents were not paid their salaries. <break time="0.8s" /> And so, as a child, I saw jam disappear from the breakfast table, then margarine disappeared, then bread became too expensive, then milk became rationed. <break time="0.8s" /> And most of all, a kind of normalized political fear invaded our lives. <break time="0.8s" /> All of these stories make me who I am. <break time="0.8s" /> But to insist on only these negative stories is to flatten my experience, and to overlook the many other stories that formed me. <break time="0.8s" /> The single story creates stereotypes. <break time="0.8s" /> And the problem with stereotypes is not that they are untrue, but that they are incomplete. <break time="0.8s" /> They make one story become the only story. <break time="0.8s" /> Of course, Africa is a continent full of catastrophes. <break time="0.8s" /> There are immense ones, such as the horrific rapes in Congo. <break time="0.8s" /> And depressing ones, such as the fact that 5, 000 people apply for one job vacancy in Nigeria.
